text: A change that's passed UAT still has to actually get into Production safely, and stay there. This lesson covers the machinery that moves code from a Git commit to a live deployment.

CI, Continuous Integration, means every commit automatically triggers a build and a test run the instant it's pushed, without a human kicking it off — that's what catches you broke something elsewhere before a human has to find it by hand. CD, Continuous Delivery or Deployment, means a change that passes CI is automatically packaged and, in a full Continuous Deployment setup, promoted all the way to Production.

A real pipeline usually has one more stop than Commit, Build, Test, Deploy suggests: Code Commit, Automated Tests, Build, Deploy to Staging, then Deploy to Production. Staging is a separate, production-like environment that catches problems automated tests alone might miss, without putting real users at risk.

A pipeline doesn't remove every judgment call. A real release still needs approval from someone with authority, monitoring watching the system right after it lands, a tested rollback plan if something goes wrong, and release notes recording what changed for both users and whoever debugs it later. Skipping any of these just moves the cost to two hours at 2 AM trying to remember what changed.

Flipping a change on for a hundred percent of users at once is the riskiest way to deploy it. Blue-green keeps two identical environments and flips traffic instantly. Canary ships to a small slice of users first. Rolling updates instances a few at a time. And feature flags let code ship dark, then get switched on independently of the deployment itself.
Next lesson: a real-world project simulation — putting Agile planning, a Kanban board, the Dev-QA-UAT-Prod chain, and a release all together on one piece of work.
